title: Hazards and uses of radioactive emissions and of background radiation (physics only)
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Physics (8463) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.4.3-c09, 4.4.3-c03, 4.4.3-c08, 4.4.3-c05. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Sievert (Sv)
items.clue: The unit of exposure risk, often quoted in thousandths.

items.label: Cosmic rays
items.clue: Ionising radiation that arrives at the Earth from space.

items.label: Radiation dose
items.clue: A measure of the risk of harm to the body from exposure.

items.label: Fallout
items.clue: Radioactive material thrown into the atmosphere by nuclear weapons testing or by a nuclear accident, which then settles onto the ground and onto vegetation over a wide area.

questions.stem: Which statement about background radiation is correct?

options.text: It is around us all of the time, from natural and from man-made sources.
It is present only in an area that a nuclear accident has affected.
It exists only because people have built reactors and weapons.
It is found only in places where uranium-bearing rock lies.

questions.explanation: Background radiation is continuously present, and it has both natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space and man-made sources such as fallout.

questions.stem: Which statement about the half-life values of radioactive isotopes is correct?

options.text: They are all much the same, since every unstable nucleus decays at a similar rate.
They all lie between a few seconds and a few days, for any isotope at all.
They change with the temperature and the pressure a sample is kept at.
They cover a very wide range, from fractions of a second to billions of years.

questions.explanation: The specification states that radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values.

questions.stem: A tracer is injected so that a doctor can watch how a patient's kidneys are working. Which property makes an isotope suitable for this use?

options.text: It emits alpha radiation, which is easily detected through the skin.
It has a half-life of many years, so the scan could be repeated later.
It emits radiation intense enough to destroy the tissue it reaches.
It emits gamma radiation, which leaves the body and is detected outside.

questions.explanation: Gamma radiation is penetrating and weakly ionising, so it passes out to a detector while depositing comparatively little energy in the patient.

questions.stem: Which of these is a natural source of background radiation?

options.text: Fallout still present from earlier nuclear weapons tests
Cosmic rays that reach the Earth's surface from space
Radioactive waste kept in a store at a power plant
Radiation produced by an X-ray machine in a hospital

questions.explanation: Cosmic rays from space are named in the specification as a natural source of background radiation, alongside rocks.

questions.stem: A radioactive isotope with a half-life of many thousands of years is spilled onto open ground. Why is such a long half-life a particular hazard here?

options.text: The ground stays radioactive for a very long time after the spill.
Its activity is enormous, so it emits a great deal of radiation now.
Isotopes with a long half-life always emit alpha, the worst kind of all.
It decays so fast that it spreads over the whole area at once.

questions.explanation: A long half-life means the activity falls only very slowly, so the contamination remains a hazard for generations.

questions.stem: How are nuclear radiations used to control or destroy a tumour lying deep inside the body?

options.text: A high dose of gamma radiation is aimed at the tumour from outside.
A weak alpha source is swallowed and travels to the tumour site itself.
A gamma source is placed so precisely that it harms only the tumour and nothing else.
The tumour is cooled by radiation until its cells stop dividing.

questions.explanation: External beam radiotherapy uses a high dose of penetrating gamma radiation directed at the tumour, often rotated around the patient.

questions.stem: An accident at a nuclear power station releases radioactive material that settles over nearby farmland. How should this contribution to the background radiation there be classified?

options.text: As natural, because the isotopes also occur in rocks
As natural, since the fallout now lies in soil
As man-made, because human activity released it
As neither, because the material has spread widely

questions.explanation: The specification lists the fallout from nuclear accidents as a man-made source; the classification depends on origin, not on where the material ends up.

questions.stem: A source with a half-life of a few minutes is spilled in a school laboratory. Why is it a serious hazard at once but much less of one an hour later?

options.text: The nuclei all stop decaying once one half-life has gone by.
Its activity is high at first and then falls away fast.
A short half-life means it gives out no radiation at all.
Its radiation changes from gamma into harmless alpha rays.

questions.explanation: A short half-life means very many decays each second at the start, and that rate halves every few minutes, so the hazard is immediate but brief.

questions.stem: A gamma-emitting tracer with a half-life of about six hours is chosen instead of one with a half-life of several years. Evaluate this choice.

options.text: Poor: a source that decays this quickly cannot give out enough radiation to be detected.
Good: the activity falls quickly, so the patient's dose after the scan stays small.
It makes no difference: once inside, you stay radioactive for life whatever the half-life.
Poor: a longer-lived tracer would let the doctors scan the same organ again later.

questions.stem: Which pair are both man-made sources of background radiation?

options.text: Cosmic rays from space and rocks lying in the earth
Rocks in the ground and waste from nuclear accidents
Cosmic rays from space and fallout from weapons tests
Fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents

questions.explanation: These are exactly the two man-made sources named in the specification.

questions.stem: A gamma beam rotated around a patient destroys a deep tumour, but it also passes through healthy tissue. Evaluate this treatment.

options.text: Justified: the tumour is destroyed and the dose to healthy tissue is limited.
Ideal: careful aiming means that only the tumour receives any radiation.
Unjustified: no dose of nuclear radiation to a patient is acceptable.
Ineffective: gamma is too weakly ionising to damage a deep tumour.

questions.explanation: Rotating the beam spreads the dose to healthy tissue over a large volume while the tumour stays in the path, so the benefit outweighs the side effects.

questions.stem: A radiographer in a hospital records a higher annual radiation dose than an office worker who lives in the same street. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Everyone receives the same dose, so the readings must be faulty.
Her occupation exposes her to radiation that the office worker never meets.
Radiation collects in the body of anybody who works indoors all day.
Both really get equal doses, so the extra reading must come from the building.

questions.explanation: The specification states that radiation dose may be affected by occupation; work with X-ray equipment and radioactive sources adds to her dose.
